q1.q: How is restaurant POS different from retail POS?
q1.a: Restaurants need tables, add-ons, kitchen routing, and peak tempo—far more than scan-and-pay retail checkout.

q2.q: Do small shops need a restaurant POS?
q2.a: If you already have busy peaks, delivery, or expansion plans, systemizing earlier avoids a full rip-and-replace later.

q3.a: It depends on menu complexity and hardware. Success is measured by clean kitchen flow and staff readiness, not just a date.

q4.q: Why do chains need restaurant POS more?
q4.a: Multi-store pain is menu drift, siloed inventory, and blind HQ. A good POS pushes decisions storewide.

q5.a: Hotpot, Chinese dining, hybrids, and stores that need QR/tableside or kitchen routing. Book a demo with your menu to confirm.

qrOrdering.metaDescription: How QR ordering works for restaurants. TAKOPOS sends guest orders to the kitchen, cuts missed tickets, and frees staff for real service.
qrOrdering.h1: QR ordering: fewer missed tickets, more real service
qrOrdering.lead: At peak, staff should not copy every order by hand. QR and tableside ordering put repeat ordering into the system so tickets reach POS and kitchen while people focus on guests.
qrOrdering.whatBody1: Guests scan a table QR code to browse the menu, add items, and leave notes. It does not replace hospitality—it removes the most repetitive peak-hour work.
qrOrdering.whatBody2: TAKOPOS connects QR ordering with POS and kitchen display so tickets appear in the kitchen immediately and floor staff stay in sync.

p1.title: No fighting for one device
p1.body: Many tables order at once without queuing for a tablet.

p2.title: Straight to the kitchen
p2.body: Less paper and verbal relay; status can return to the floor.

p3.title: Language & notes built in
p3.body: Tourists and custom requests need fewer back-and-forth checks.

p4.title: Service back at the table
p4.body: Staff spend time on care and recommendations, not transcription.

q1.q: Will QR ordering make service colder?
q1.a: Automate copying tickets; keep people for hospitality. Most stores see fewer complaints and faster turns.

q2.a: No. Mix handheld tableside ordering with QR by daypart and table type.

q3.a: Same stack is safer. Split vendors often fail at peak; TAKOPOS keeps one flow.

q4.a: Hotpot, yakiniku, multi-course, and bars with heavy add-ons feel it first.

kitchenDisplay.metaDescription: What a kitchen display should do at peak. TAKOPOS KDS routes by station with clear status to cut missed tickets and shouting.
kitchenDisplay.h1: Kitchen display (KDS): less shouting, clearer plating
kitchenDisplay.lead: Flying paper tickets and verbal chases create peak complaints. KDS puts orders on screen by station so everyone knows the next step.
kitchenDisplay.whatBody1: A KDS replaces or backs paper tickets with live screens for queued, in-progress, and done items—optionally split by grill, fry, drinks, and more.
kitchenDisplay.whatBody2: Tied to POS and QR ordering, front-of-house tickets hit the kitchen instantly and completion can signal the floor.
kitchenDisplay.pointsTitle: What KDS should carry for the kitchen

p1.title: Route by station
p1.body: Each station sees its own work—fewer collisions and misses.

p2.title: Transparent status

p3.title: Peak item bundling
p3.body: Same items can aggregate for faster prep.

p4.title: Fewer remakes
p4.body: Notes and add-ons stop relying on verbal relay.

q1.a: If peak already means misses or shouting, even one screen on the main station helps.

q2.a: Anything marked Live can be demoed; Planned ships on the product roadmap.

q3.a: It cuts cataloging, translation, stocktake, and triage time so people focus on guests and decisions.

q4.q: How is AI priced? Any new-customer credit?
q4.a: Pay as you go by usage points. New customers get 100 free points to try menu setup, translation, and more.

tposAiPage.ctaTitle: Want AI on your real menu?
tposAiPage.ctaBody: Book an intro with a live menu—we will walk setup, translation, and reports.
